column1: # What the reference's archive test suite runs, one row per case. The keys are
# the reference's own case names — from `--gtest_list_tests` on the suite built
# at 664f58e705, the list the acceptance run uses as its denominator (review
# E-3: pin the set of names, not a count).
# It exists because the archive is a pure-Rust implementation and the reference
# suite cannot be its test suite: that suite needs a reference checkout, a CMake
# build, the shim and a JDK, and takes seven minutes serialised. So the two do
# different jobs — this file is the denominator for *ours*, and the reference
# suite is the instrument for "can it replace the Java archive at all".
#   kind        system      exercises the archive server; the port target
# Nothing is ever deleted: a case the reference drops, or one this build decides
# is not its business, is an edit to make deliberately, with the count moved in
# ★ The ownership columns are gone, and the reason is worth keeping. Until
# `reference-only`) and `covered_by`, under a growth rule: *a P2 slice that
# lands a scenario flips its row from `pending` to `ported` and names the test*.
# **Four slices went by and not one row was flipped**, and not out of laziness:
# which of this build's tests "owns" which reference case is a human judgement,
# so no gate could ever fail on it, and a promise nothing checks loses to
# everything that something checks. What records coverage is the **acceptance
# run** — one row per case name, in the TSV it writes under `analysis/archive/`
# — and a hand-kept second copy of that was never once consulted. The
# denominator, which is what `suite.rs` actually guards, was doing the work all
# along; this is the shape `reference-java-cases.tsv` has always had.
